Miasma infectHost persistence in AI coding assistant configs AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the infectHost routine that backdoors AI coding-assistant configuration files for re-execution: .claude/settings.json (SessionStart hook), .vscode/tasks.json (folderOpen), .cursor/rules/, .aider.conf.yml, and .github/copilot-instructions.md. Filters to writes performed by node/bun/npm so legit editor saves are excluded. Rationale: Directly maps the article's infectHost target list (Claude Code SessionStart hook in .claude/settings.json, VS Code folderOpen in .vscode/tasks.json, .cursor/rules, .aider.conf.yml, .github/copilot-instructions.md); requiring a node/bun writer separates the malware from legitimate IDE saves. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/immobiliarelabs-npm-packages-compromised • https://semgrep.dev/blog/2026/miasma-v2-self-spreading-npm-worm-now-uses-malicious-bindinggyp-file-and-compromises-57-packages/
ATT&CKT1546 T1554
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A developer's VS Code / Cursor extension (which runs under node) legitimately writing tasks.json or rules on project open
  • Aider itself updating .aider.conf.yml during normal use
  • Dotfile-management tooling (chezmoi/yadm) restoring AI-assistant configs
  • An MCP/agent framework legitimately writing a SessionStart hook into .claude/settings.json
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("code","cursor","aider") and InitiatingProcessParentFileName in~ ("code","cursor"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: open the written config and inspect the hook/command body — Miasma injects a shell/JS command into the SessionStart, folderOpen, or rules entry; benign saves contain no execution directive. 2) Contain: revert the config from version control, remove the injected hook, and isolate the host if a command was present. 3) Hunt: enumerate every repo/home dir on the host for the same five config files, and check whether the SessionStart hook already fired (child processes of the AI assistant).
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| where FolderPath has_any ("/.claude/settings.json", "/.vscode/tasks.json", "/.cursor/rules", "/.aider.conf.yml", "copilot-instructions.md") or FileName in~ ("settings.json","tasks.json",".aider.conf.yml","copilot-instructions.md")
| where FolderPath has_any (".claude",".vscode",".cursor",".aider.conf.yml","copilot-instructions.md")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node","bun","sh","bash","dash","npm","node-gyp")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ActionType, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| where TargetFilePath has_any (".claude/settings.json", ".vscode/tasks.json", ".cursor/rules", ".aider.conf.yml", "copilot-instructions.md")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("node","bun","sh","bash","dash","npm","node-gyp")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Cloud instance-metadata harvesting from npm/node install context (Miasma credential theft) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the Miasma harvester reaching AWS IMDS (169.254.169.254) or ECS task-metadata (169.254.170.2) from a node/bun/npm/node-gyp process — the exact endpoints the article lists for cloud credential theft. Scoped to install-tooling parents and the Bun stage so it isn't a long-running app's normal SDK traffic. Rationale: Uses the article's literal credential-source endpoints (IMDS 169.254.169.254 and ECS metadata 169.254.170.2) tied to the npm/node/Bun execution context; metadata access from package-install tooling (vs a steady-state app) is the high-fidelity differentiator. Sentinel left empty because ImNetworkSession carries no initiating-process attribution to bind the IMDS hit to node/bun. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/binding-gyp-npm-supply-chain-attack-spreads-like-worm • https://www.wiz.io/blog/miasma-supply-chain-attack-targeting-redhat-npm-packages
ATT&CKT1552.005 T1552.007
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A Node.js app on EC2/ECS legitimately using the AWS SDK to refresh instance-role credentials via IMDS
  • CI tooling (e.g. node-based deploy scripts) that queries instance identity at job start
  • Container health agents written in node polling task metadata
  • Infra-as-code node CLIs (CDK) resolving region/account from IMDS
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "aws-sdk" and InitiatingProcessParentFileName !in~ ("systemd","pm2","forever")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the calling process lineage — IMDS access from a process whose parent is npm/node-gyp/sh during a package install, or from a Bun temp process, is not normal SDK usage. 2) Contain: isolate the host/runner and immediately rotate the instance-role / task-role credentials and any cloud keys reachable from that role; review CloudTrail for use of those creds from new IPs. 3) Hunt: check for follow-on reads of /proc/<Runner.Worker pid>/mem, Vault token files (/home/runner/.vault-token, /root/.vault-token, /run/secrets/VAULT_TOKEN), and .ssh/ on the same host.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteIP in ("169.254.169.254","169.254.170.2")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("bun","node","npm","node-gyp","sh","bash","dash","yarn","pnpm")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "bun" or InitiatingProcessParentFileName in~ ("npm","node-gyp","sh","bash","dash","yarn","pnpm")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc

Compromised @immobiliarelabs Backstage plugin on disk (binding.gyp + index.js / known hashes) AIDelivery Medium
Inventory/IOC detection for the trojanized @immobiliarelabs/backstage-plugin-gitlab(-backend) and backstage-plugin-ldap-auth(-backend) packages. Clean releases never shipped a binding.gyp, so the presence of binding.gyp or the 5 MB index.js inside those package paths — or any file matching the three published malicious SHA256s — confirms a compromised version was installed. Rationale: Built on the article's affected-package matrix plus the three published SHA256 IOCs; a binding.gyp inside these specific Backstage plugin directories is itself anomalous because the clean 2.1.1-era releases shipped neither binding.gyp nor a 5 MB index.js. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/immobiliarelabs-npm-packages-compromised • https://vulnerability.circl.lu/vuln/mal-2026-6527 • https://snyk.io/blog/node-gyp-supply-chain-compromise-self-propagating-npm-worm-binding-gyp/
ATT&CKT1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security team intentionally staging the malicious tarball in an isolated analysis sandbox
  • A cached npm tarball retained on a build agent after remediation (already-known, low risk)
  • An offline mirror/proxy (Verdaccio/Artifactory) holding a quarantined copy for inspection
  • Hash collision is implausible — SHA256 matches are definitive
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the exact package@version from the path against the affected matrix (gitlab/gitlab-backend 3.0.3–7.0.2, 1.0.1, 2.1.2; ldap-auth(-backend) 1.1.3/1.1.4–5.2.1) and check whether node-gyp executed it (install actually ran). 2) Contain: pin/roll back to a known-clean version, purge the tarball from caches and lockfiles, isolate affected build agents, and rotate every credential reachable from that host/CI job. 3) Hunt: pivot to binding.gyp execution, Bun temp execution, IMDS access, and AI-assistant config writes on the same hosts; sweep the registry/repo org for republished (worm-propagated) packages from any maintainer account touched by these runners.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where (FolderPath has "@immobiliarelabs" and (FolderPath has "backstage-plugin-gitlab" or FolderPath has "backstage-plugin-ldap-auth") and FileName in~ ("binding.gyp","index.js"))
    or SHA256 in~ ("ceff7c51d70832c3ec8dd2744b606a23b3c924ef664ae23439b9b742ea154108","da39146ef451d1b174a24d00b1e2a45cd38d54e849737f8f35333dcb22175707","ef641e956f91d501b748085996303c96a64d67f63bfeef0dda175e5aa19cca90")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, FileName, FileSize, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where (TargetFilePath has "@immobiliarelabs" and (TargetFilePath has "backstage-plugin-gitlab" or TargetFilePath has "backstage-plugin-ldap-auth") and TargetFileName in~ ("binding.gyp","index.js"))
    or TargetFileSHA256 in~ ("ceff7c51d70832c3ec8dd2744b606a23b3c924ef664ae23439b9b742ea154108","da39146ef451d1b174a24d00b1e2a45cd38d54e849737f8f35333dcb22175707","ef641e956f91d501b748085996303c96a64d67f63bfeef0dda175e5aa19cca90")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, TargetFileSHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("ceff7c51d70832c3ec8dd2744b606a23b3c924ef664ae23439b9b742ea154108", "da39146ef451d1b174a24d00b1e2a45cd38d54e849737f8f35333dcb22175707", "ef641e956f91d501b748085996303c96a64d67f63bfeef0dda175e5aa19cca90") or SHA1 in~ ("ceff7c51d70832c3ec8dd2744b606a23b3c924ef664ae23439b9b742ea154108", "da39146ef451d1b174a24d00b1e2a45cd38d54e849737f8f35333dcb22175707", "ef641e956f91d501b748085996303c96a64d67f63bfeef0dda175e5aa19cca90") or MD5 in~ ("ceff7c51d70832c3ec8dd2744b606a23b3c924ef664ae23439b9b742ea154108", "da39146ef451d1b174a24d00b1e2a45cd38d54e849737f8f35333dcb22175707", "ef641e956f91d501b748085996303c96a64d67f63bfeef0dda175e5aa19cca90")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("ceff7c51d70832c3ec8dd2744b606a23b3c924ef664ae23439b9b742ea154108", "da39146ef451d1b174a24d00b1e2a45cd38d54e849737f8f35333dcb22175707", "ef641e956f91d501b748085996303c96a64d67f63bfeef0dda175e5aa19cca90") or SHA1 in~ ("ceff7c51d70832c3ec8dd2744b606a23b3c924ef664ae23439b9b742ea154108", "da39146ef451d1b174a24d00b1e2a45cd38d54e849737f8f35333dcb22175707", "ef641e956f91d501b748085996303c96a64d67f63bfeef0dda175e5aa19cca90") or MD5 in~ ("ceff7c51d70832c3ec8dd2744b606a23b3c924ef664ae23439b9b742ea154108", "da39146ef451d1b174a24d00b1e2a45cd38d54e849737f8f35333dcb22175707", "ef641e956f91d501b748085996303c96a64d67f63bfeef0dda175e5aa19cca90")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["ceff7c51d70832c3ec8dd2744b606a23b3c924ef664ae23439b9b742ea154108", "da39146ef451d1b174a24d00b1e2a45cd38d54e849737f8f35333dcb22175707", "ef641e956f91d501b748085996303c96a64d67f63bfeef0dda175e5aa19cca90"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Jackson Maven typosquat C2 — beacon to fasterxml.org / 103.127.243.82 AICommand & Control High
Hunts hosts resolving or connecting to the namespace-impersonation C2 (fasterxml.org / m.fasterxml.org) or the staging IP 103.127.243.82 used by the malicious org.fasterxml.jackson.core:jackson-databind artifact to pull a Cobalt Strike beacon. Article-specific: these are typosquats of the legitimate fasterxml.com / com.fasterxml namespace, so any hit is high-fidelity. Rationale: fasterxml.org / m.fasterxml.org and 103.127.243.82:8000 are the verbatim C2 from Aikido's analysis (config.txt + svchosts.exe staging), typosquatting the real fasterxml.com — so any resolution/connection is malicious by definition. Cross-checked Aikido and cybersecuritynews/SC Media. Cross-checked against: • https://www.aikido.dev/blog/maven-central-jackson-typosquatting-malware • https://cybersecuritynews.com/hackers-infiltrated-maven-central/ • https://www.scworld.com/brief/maven-central-subjected-to-typosquatted-jackson-json-library
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1105
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Malware-analysis sandbox or researcher detonating the sample in-house
  • Threat-intel proxy / URL-crawler pre-resolving the IOC domain
  • DNS sinkhole or RPZ responding to the domain (benign, but worth confirming sink not real resolve)
  • Internal artifact-mirror health-check probing the coordinate's declared SCM/URL
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe") // exclude analyst browser lookups of the IOC
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the InitiatingProcess (expect java.exe/javaw.exe from a Spring Boot app or CI runner); confirm whether the resolve led to an actual TCP connect to 103.127.243.82:8000 or :51211. 2) Contain: isolate the host, block fasterxml.org / m.fasterxml.org / 103.127.243.82 at egress, and pull the build's dependency tree for org.fasterxml.jackson.core:jackson-databind. 3) Hunt: sweep all CI runners and dev machines that resolved org.fasterxml namespace coordinates, and pivot to UC2/UC3 for dropped svchosts.exe / payload.bin and the two SHA256 implants.

| where RemoteUrl has "fasterxml.org" or RemoteIP == "103.127.243.82"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc

| order by TimeGenerated desc

Java/Spring drops & runs svchosts.exe (svchost masquerade) — Jackson typosquat implant AIInstallation High
Hunts the second-stage drop where the malicious JacksonSpringAutoConfiguration class writes payload.bin to temp and executes svchosts.exe (a typosquat of the legitimate svchost.exe). Article-specific via the exact filenames and the java.exe→svchosts.exe parent/child chain. Rationale: svchosts.exe (note trailing 's') is never a legitimate Windows binary and is the verbatim Windows payload name; pairing the java.exe parent with the two confirmed SHA256 implants makes this near-zero-FP. Sourced from Aikido's payload breakdown. Cross-checked against: • https://www.aikido.dev/blog/maven-central-jackson-typosquatting-malware • https://cybersecuritynews.com/hackers-infiltrated-maven-central/
ATT&CKT1105 T1036.005 T1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer or pentester naming an unrelated test binary svchosts.exe
  • Red-team tooling intentionally masquerading as svchost
  • Unrelated commodity malware reusing the svchosts.exe name (still malicious — escalate)
  • EDR sample-replay / detonation lab running the captured artifact
Suppression filter
| where not(FolderPath has_any (@"\Tests\", @"\redteam\")) // suppress sanctioned test/red-team binaries
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the binary path (expect a temp/working dir, not System32) and parent (java.exe/javaw.exe from a Spring Boot app or CI build); validate SHA256 against the two known implant hashes. 2) Contain: kill the process, isolate the host, and quarantine svchosts.exe / payload.bin; block the C2 from UC1. 3) Hunt: search the host and peers for the hidden .idea.pid persistence marker, for beacons to 103.127.243.82:8000 / m.fasterxml.org:51211, and audit which builds resolved org.fasterxml.jackson.core:jackson-databind.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "svchosts.exe"
   or SHA256 in ("8bce95ebfb895537fec243e069d7193980361de9d916339906b11a14ffded94f","702161756dfd150ad3c214fbf97ce98fdc960ea7b3970b5300702ed8c953cafd")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetProcessName has "svchosts.exe"
   or (ParentProcessName has_any ("java.exe","javaw.exe") and TargetProcessName has "svchosts.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, TargetProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Jackson typosquat Cobalt Strike implant hash sighting (Win + macOS/Linux) AIInstallation Medium
Vector-agnostic sweep for the two confirmed implant SHA256 hashes (svchosts.exe for Windows, 'update' for macOS/Linux) dropped by the malicious jackson-databind artifact. Catches the implant even when delivered outside the java→svchosts.exe chain (e.g. pulled directly into a CI cache). Rationale: The two SHA256 are the verbatim VirusTotal-confirmed Cobalt Strike beacons (Windows svchosts.exe + macOS/Linux 'update') from Aikido's IOC list; an exact-hash match is effectively zero-FP and covers non-Windows hosts the process/network UCs miss. Cross-checked against: • https://www.aikido.dev/blog/maven-central-jackson-typosquatting-malware • https://www.scworld.com/brief/maven-central-subjected-to-typosquatted-jackson-json-library

  • Backup/forensic image containing a previously quarantined copy
  • Sandbox detonation lab re-fetching the sample

1) Triage: confirm the writing process and path — distinguish an AV/EDR quarantine vault (benign) from a live drop in a build/temp dir (true positive). 2) Contain: isolate the host, quarantine the file, and revoke any CI/cloud credentials reachable from the build that pulled jackson-databind (Cobalt Strike harvests CI secrets). 3) Hunt: pivot to UC1 (C2 to fasterxml.org / 103.127.243.82) and UC2 (svchosts.exe execution) on the same and neighbouring hosts, and inventory every repo/runner that resolved org.fasterxml.jackson.core coordinates.

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`

| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count

title: Obfuscated / Encoded PowerShell Execution
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d08
status: experimental
description: |
    PowerShell launched with -EncodedCommand, base64 strings, hidden
    window, no-profile, bypass policy, IEX / Invoke-Expression / Net
    .WebClient.DownloadString — combinations indicating evasion.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1027/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059.001
    - attack.t1027
    - attack.execution
    - attack.defense-evasion
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_image:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
    selection_args:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - '-enc '
            - 'EncodedCommand'
            - 'FromBase64String'
            - 'Invoke-Expression'
            - 'IEX('
            - 'DownloadString'
            - 'Net.WebClient'
            - '-w hidden'
            - '-WindowStyle Hidden'
            - '-nop'
            - '-NoProfile'
            - '-ep bypass'
            - '-ExecutionPolicy Bypass'
    condition: selection_image and selection_args
falsepositives:
    - DevOps tooling that legitimately uses encoded command for
      cross-shell escaping
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*-enc *" OR Processes.process="*EncodedCommand*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64String*" OR Processes.process="*-nop*"
        OR Processes.process="*-w hidden*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*IEX(*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*Net.WebClient*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*-enc *" OR Processes.process="*EncodedCommand*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64String*" OR Processes.process="*-nop*"
        OR Processes.process="*-w hidden*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*IEX(*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*Net.WebClient*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

DeviceProcessEvents

| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
// Replace `"setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe"` with the vendor binaries observed in the
// article (matching shape with the Defender query).
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)

| where ParentProcessName has_any ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\rundll32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\regsvr32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe"

| order by TimeGenerated desc

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("8bce95ebfb895537fec243e069d7193980361de9d916339906b11a14ffded94f", "702161756dfd150ad3c214fbf97ce98fdc960ea7b3970b5300702ed8c953cafd") or SHA1 in~ ("8bce95ebfb895537fec243e069d7193980361de9d916339906b11a14ffded94f", "702161756dfd150ad3c214fbf97ce98fdc960ea7b3970b5300702ed8c953cafd") or MD5 in~ ("8bce95ebfb895537fec243e069d7193980361de9d916339906b11a14ffded94f", "702161756dfd150ad3c214fbf97ce98fdc960ea7b3970b5300702ed8c953cafd")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("8bce95ebfb895537fec243e069d7193980361de9d916339906b11a14ffded94f", "702161756dfd150ad3c214fbf97ce98fdc960ea7b3970b5300702ed8c953cafd") or SHA1 in~ ("8bce95ebfb895537fec243e069d7193980361de9d916339906b11a14ffded94f", "702161756dfd150ad3c214fbf97ce98fdc960ea7b3970b5300702ed8c953cafd") or MD5 in~ ("8bce95ebfb895537fec243e069d7193980361de9d916339906b11a14ffded94f", "702161756dfd150ad3c214fbf97ce98fdc960ea7b3970b5300702ed8c953cafd")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["8bce95ebfb895537fec243e069d7193980361de9d916339906b11a14ffded94f", "702161756dfd150ad3c214fbf97ce98fdc960ea7b3970b5300702ed8c953cafd"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

High

Mass npm Supply Chain Attack: 20 Leo Platform Packages Compromised

StepSecurity
2026-07-01 7 use cases 3 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

On June 24, 2026, an attacker published malicious versions of 20 npm packages belonging to the Leo Platform ecosystem in a coordinated burst spanning less than three seconds. All 20 packages carry an identical CI/CD attack toolkit that steals secrets from GitHub Actions runners, cloud credential stores, package registries, and password managers, then exfiltrates them via the victim's own GitHub token. Together these packages receive approximately 13,600 downloads per week.

Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Bun executes dropped temp payload /tmp/p*.js (Miasma stealer launch) · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Mass npm Supply Chain Attack: 20 Leo Platform Packages Compromised
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Passwordless sudo backdoor written for runner account (runner ALL=(ALL) NOPASSWD:ALL) · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Bun v1.3.13 runtime pulled from GitHub Releases during npm install (Phantom Gyp staging)
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] GitHub Actions Runner.Worker memory read via /proc/<pid>/mem (CI secret unmasking)
Bun v1.3.13 runtime pulled from GitHub Releases during npm install (Phantom Gyp staging) AICommand & Control High
Hunts the Leo Platform / Miasma toolkit fetching the pinned Bun v1.3.13 single-file binary from github.com/oven-sh/bun/releases during a node/npm install. The stealer runs its core logic under this downloaded Bun runtime specifically to evade Node-child monitoring, so an install-context process reaching this exact release URL is a high-fidelity stager signal. Rationale: Anchored on the article's exact version-pinned Bun download URL (github.com/oven-sh/bun/releases/download/bun-v1.3.13/) scoped to install-tooling initiators; Snyk and Microsoft both confirm the downloaded-Bun evasion for the same toolkit. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/binding-gyp-npm-supply-chain-attack-spreads-like-worm • https://snyk.io/blog/bun-based-stealer-hits-sap-cap-js-mbt-npm-packages/ • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/05/20/mini-shai-hulud-compromised-antv-npm-packages-enable-ci-cd-credential-theft/
ATT&CKT1105 T1195.002
Data sourcesWeb.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate projects that genuinely vendor Bun v1.3.13 and download it during CI build (e.g. Bun-based test suites)
  • Internal mirror/proxy caching the Bun release that then serves it to many build agents
  • Developer manually pinning bun-v1.3.13 in a setup script invoked by npm postinstall of a trusted package
  • Renovate/Dependabot dry-run installs that fetch toolchains
Suppression filter
| where not(InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("bun-types","@biomejs") and DeviceName startswith "trusted-bun-ci")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the package + version being installed when the download fired (correlate InitiatingProcessCommandLine / build log) and confirm whether the repo legitimately uses Bun; check the host against the 20 Leo Platform packages and the 2026-06-24T23:04:55Z publish window. 2) Contain: isolate/cordon the runner, revoke the GITHUB_TOKEN and any cloud creds (AWS/GCP/Azure/Vault) reachable from it, and rotate npm publish tokens for accounts that ran the build. 3) Hunt: pivot on the same host/account for bun executing /tmp/p*.js, /proc/<pid>/mem reads of Runner.Worker, and sudoers NOPASSWD writes; search the org for any leo-* package at the malicious versions in package-lock files.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("oven-sh/bun/releases/download/bun-v1.3.13", "bun-v1.3.13")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node","npm","node-gyp","bun","yarn","pnpm")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Url has_any ("oven-sh/bun/releases/download/bun-v1.3.13", "bun-v1.3.13")
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname, SrcUsername, Url, UserAgent = HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent, DstHostname, DvcAction
| order by TimeGenerated desc

GitHub Actions Runner.Worker memory read via /proc/<pid>/mem (CI secret unmasking) AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts the toolkit locating the GitHub Actions Runner.Worker process and reading /proc/<pid>/mem directly (sometimes via a sudo python3 helper) to recover secrets that are masked in workflow logs. Reading another process's /proc memory on a CI runner is definitively malicious and is the campaign's core credential-access step. Rationale: Uses the article's definitive CI indicator (read of /proc/{pid}/mem where the target is Runner.Worker); the regex on /proc/<pid>/mem captures both the direct-read and sudo-python3 helper variants documented by Microsoft for the same toolkit. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/binding-gyp-npm-supply-chain-attack-spreads-like-worm • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/05/20/mini-shai-hulud-compromised-antv-npm-packages-enable-ci-cd-credential-theft/
ATT&CKT1003.007 T1212
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate debuggers/profilers (gdb, perf, gcore) attaching to a process during a build-time crash dump
  • Container/runtime health tooling snapshotting memory for diagnostics
  • Security agents themselves enumerating /proc (allowlist the EDR/AV process)
  • Coredump collection scripts that copy /proc/<pid>/mem ranges
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("gdb","gcore","perf","mdatp","wdavdaemon","crash")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the reader is NOT a known debugger/EDR and that the target PID resolves to Runner.Worker (check /proc/<pid>/cmdline access just before); treat any read in a GitHub Actions context as confirmed. 2) Contain: kill the runner, revoke the workflow GITHUB_TOKEN/OIDC token immediately and rotate every secret exposed to that workflow (cloud keys, registry tokens, 1Password items). 3) Hunt: look for the preceding Bun v1.3.13 download and subsequent GitHub GraphQL writes to newly-created dead-drop repos under the build's own token, and check for npm bypass_2fa republish activity.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"/proc/[0-9]+/mem"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where SyslogMessage matches regex @"/proc/[0-9]+/mem"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Facility, ProcessName, ProcessID, SyslogMessage
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Passwordless sudo backdoor written for runner account (runner ALL=(ALL) NOPASSWD:ALL) AIInstallation High
Hunts the toolkit granting itself passwordless sudo on GitHub-hosted runners by writing 'runner ALL=(ALL) NOPASSWD:ALL' into the sudoers configuration. The exact account+NOPASSWD string is a narrow, high-fidelity privilege-escalation indicator unique to this campaign's runner targeting. Rationale: Anchored on the article's verbatim escalation string 'runner ALL=(ALL) NOPASSWD:ALL'; matching NOPASSWD:ALL plus the runner principal keeps it tight to this campaign's GitHub-hosted-runner targeting rather than generic sudoers edits. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/mass-npm-supply-chain-attack-20-leo-platform-packages-compromised • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/binding-gyp-npm-supply-chain-attack-spreads-like-worm
ATT&CKT1548.003 T1098
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Provisioning/IaC (Ansible, cloud-init) that legitimately grants the runner/build user NOPASSWD sudo on self-hosted runners
  • Container base-image build steps adding a NOPASSWD entry for a service account named runner
  • Admins troubleshooting sudo on a CI host
  • Vendor runner setup scripts that intentionally configure passwordless sudo
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("ansible","cloud-init","python3-ansible","chef-client","puppet")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm whether the sudoers write originated from a known provisioning tool/parent (Ansible, cloud-init) or from a build/npm-install descendant; the latter is malicious. 2) Contain: remove the sudoers entry, terminate the runner, and rotate credentials reachable from it; for ephemeral GitHub-hosted runners assume the runner is fully compromised and tear it down. 3) Hunt: correlate with the same host's Bun v1.3.13 download, /proc/<pid>/mem reads, and any GitHub Actions workflow files modified to add id-token: write and attacker-pinned action SHAs.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ProcessCommandLine contains "NOPASSWD:ALL" and ProcessCommandLine has "runner"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetProcessCommandLine contains "NOPASSWD:ALL" and TargetProcessCommandLine has "runner"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Bun executes dropped temp payload /tmp/p*.js (Miasma stealer launch) AIExploitation High
Hunts the downloaded Bun runtime executing the toolkit's dropped payload at /tmp/p*.js — the definitive behavioral indicator that the obfuscated stealer logic has launched out-of-band from the Node install process. Bun running a script out of /tmp during a package install is anomalous and campaign-specific. Rationale: Uses the article's stated payload drop/exec location (/tmp/p*.js executed by bun) tied to the bun binary name; this parent-runtime + temp-path JS combination is the campaign's definitive behavioral execution indicator and near-zero in normal builds. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/mass-npm-supply-chain-attack-20-leo-platform-packages-compromised • https://snyk.io/blog/bun-based-stealer-hits-sap-cap-js-mbt-npm-packages/
ATT&CKT1059.007 T1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer running an ad-hoc Bun script saved under /tmp during local debugging
  • CI scratch scripts written to /tmp and executed by a Bun-based build that happen to match the p*.js pattern
  • Test harnesses that generate temp .js fixtures and run them under Bun
  • Bun's own cache/transpile artifacts if relocated to /tmp
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node","npm","node-gyp","sh","bash","yarn","pnpm")
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the /tmp/p*.js contents (or its hash) before it self-deletes and confirm the parent chain is node/npm install rather than an intentional Bun project. 2) Contain: kill the bun process and runner, revoke the workflow token and rotate all cloud/registry/Vault/1Password secrets exposed to the job. 3) Hunt: pivot to the host's outbound Bun v1.3.13 download, /proc/<pid>/mem Runner.Worker reads, sudoers NOPASSWD writes, and any npm publishes via bypass_2fa from accounts that ran the build; scan repos for leo-* packages pinned to the malicious versions.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName =~ "bun"
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"/tmp/p[^/ ]*\.js"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where TargetProcessName has "bun"
| where TargetProcessCommandLine matches regex @"/tmp/p[^/ ]*\.js"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children Exploitation Medium
Supply-chain trojan signal: legitimate signed binary spawning script interpreters or exotic LOLBins.
ATT&CKT1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
// Replace `"setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe"` with the vendor binaries observed in the
// article (matching shape with the Defender query).
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\rundll32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\regsvr32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\bitsadmin.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

simonecorsi/mawesome GitHub Action has been compromised

StepSecurity
2026-07-01 4 use cases 1 technique 3 kill-chain phases detected

On June 24, 2026, an attacker compromised the simonecorsi/mawesome GitHub repository. They force-pushed malicious commits and repointed several version tags to that commit. As a result, any workflow running against those tags after that time executed the attacker's code inside its GitHub Actions runner.

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code.
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Compromised simonecorsi/mawesome GitHub Action payload by known hash · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Runner.Worker process memory scrape via /proc on self-hosted GitHub Actions runner · [LLM] First-seen external egress from GitHub Actions Runner.Worker child process
Compromised simonecorsi/mawesome GitHub Action payload by known hash AIInstallation Medium
Hunts for the specific malicious payload pushed to simonecorsi/mawesome during the June 24 2026 tag-poisoning compromise, matched by SHA256/SHA1 on self-hosted GitHub Actions runners monitored by EDR. Fires on file write or process execution of the imposter-commit artifact inside the runner. Rationale: Pivots on the article's three pre-extracted IOCs (SHA256 9f93d77d... and the two SHA1s) which are the imposter-commit payload; a hash match is near-zero-FP, so this is a clean alerting rule for any self-hosted runner that executed a poisoned mawesome tag. Cross-checked against: • https://www.wiz.io/blog/github-action-tj-actions-changed-files-supply-chain-attack-cve-2025-30066 • https://www.sysdig.com/blog/detecting-and-mitigating-the-tj-actions-changed-files-supply-chain-attack-cve-2025-30066 • https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/alerts/2025/03/18/supply-chain-compromise-third-party-tj-actionschanged-files-cve-2025-30066-and-reviewdogaction
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1059
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security researcher detonating the sample in a sandboxed runner for analysis
  • EDR/AV quarantine copy of the file re-scanned generating a benign file event
  • Threat-intel team staging the IOC file on a host for YARA testing
  • Backup/forensic image mounting that re-reads the captured payload
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe") or FolderPath has_any ("\\Quarantine\\", "/quarantine/"))
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Confirm the host is a self-hosted GitHub Actions runner and pull the workflow run that executed it; identify which mawesome tag/SHA was referenced and the repo. 2) CONTAIN: Isolate the runner, rotate ALL secrets exposed to that workflow (GITHUB_TOKEN, cloud OIDC roles, registry creds, signing keys) and pin the action to a trusted commit SHA or remove it. 3) HUNT: Search other runners for the same hashes, review egress from the runner during the run window, and check downstream artifacts/packages built by that pipeline for tampering.

title: Compromised simonecorsi/mawesome GitHub Action Payload by Hash
id: 7c1d9a42-3b8e-4f21-9a6c-0e2f5d8b41aa
status: experimental
description: Detects execution of the malicious payload from the June 2026 simonecorsi/mawesome GitHub Action tag-poisoning compromise by known SHA256/SHA1 hash.
references:

  - https://www.wiz.io/blog/github-action-tj-actions-changed-files-supply-chain-attack-cve-2025-30066

date: 2026/06/25
tags:

  - attack.execution

detection:
  selection:
    Hashes|contains:
      - '9f93d77d32833a515bc406c46da477142bb1ac2babeecb6aa42f98669a6db015'
      - '5792aba0e2180b9b80b77644370a6889d5817456'
      - 'bcb6b1d409144318e8fad2171d6fe06d02299d1a'
  condition: selection
level: high
source:windows.sysmon (@Hashes:*9F93D77D32833A515BC406C46DA477142BB1AC2BABEECB6AA42F98669A6DB015* OR @Hashes:*9f93d77d32833a515bc406c46da477142bb1ac2babeecb6aa42f98669a6db015* OR @Hashes:*5792ABA0E2180B9B80B77644370A6889D5817456* OR @Hashes:*5792aba0e2180b9b80b77644370a6889d5817456* OR @Hashes:*BCB6B1D409144318E8FAD2171D6FE06D02299D1A* OR @Hashes:*bcb6b1d409144318e8fad2171d6fe06d02299d1a*)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2
| SHA256HashData=/9f93d77d32833a515bc406c46da477142bb1ac2babeecb6aa42f98669a6db015/i OR SHA1HashData=/5792aba0e2180b9b80b77644370a6889d5817456/i OR SHA1HashData=/bcb6b1d409144318e8fad2171d6fe06d02299d1a/i

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_hash IN ("9f93d77d32833a515bc406c46da477142bb1ac2babeecb6aa42f98669a6db015","5792aba0e2180b9b80b77644370a6889d5817456","bcb6b1d409144318e8fad2171d6fe06d02299d1a") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process_name Processes.process Processes.process_hash | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)

Runner.Worker process memory scrape via /proc on self-hosted GitHub Actions runner AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts the core mawesome/tj-actions-style payload behaviour: a child process spawned by the GitHub Actions Runner.Worker reading /proc/<pid>/maps or /proc/<pid>/mem to scrape CI/CD secrets from runner memory. Article-specific because it pivots on Runner.Worker as the parent plus the in-image label 'Runner.Worker Memory Scrape'. Rationale: Corroborated by Sysdig/Wiz analyses of the identical tj-actions payload which 'identifies the Runner.Worker process, opens its memory mappings and regex-searches for secrets'; the Runner.Worker parent + /proc maps/mem access is the high-fidelity credential-access signal the thin article only labels as 'Runner.Worker Memory Scrape'. Cross-checked against: • https://www.sysdig.com/blog/detecting-and-mitigating-the-tj-actions-changed-files-supply-chain-attack-cve-2025-30066 • https://www.wiz.io/blog/github-action-tj-actions-changed-files-supply-chain-attack-cve-2025-30066
ATT&CKT1003.007 T1552
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Runner self-diagnostic or crash-dump tooling (gcore/dd) reading worker memory during a hang
  • Performance profilers (perf, py-spy) attached to a build process inside CI
  • Custom debugging step in a workflow that intentionally inspects /proc for troubleshooting
  • Container runtime health checks reading /proc/<pid>/status (excluded by maps/mem filter)
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("py-spy","perf record","/proc/self/status","/proc/meminfo") )
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Pull the full command line of the child process and the workflow YAML that ran; confirm whether a memory-read step was legitimately authored or injected by a third-party action. 2) CONTAIN: Treat every secret available to that job as compromised — rotate tokens/OIDC roles immediately and isolate the runner from further job dispatch. 3) HUNT: Pivot on the same Runner.Worker parent across all runners for /proc memory reads, base64-encoded stdout, and any outbound POST to gist.githubusercontent.com or unknown hosts in the same run window.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has "Runner.Worker"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "/proc/" and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("maps","mem")
| where FileName in~ ("python3","python","node","perl","ruby","sh","bash","cat","dd","gcore")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where ParentProcessName has "Runner.Worker"
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has "/proc/" and ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("maps","mem")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("python3","python","node","perl","ruby","bash","sh","cat","dd","gcore")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: GitHub Actions Runner.Worker Memory Scrape via Proc Filesystem
id: b2e64f18-9c7a-4d53-8a11-6f3c20d9e7b4
status: experimental
description: Detects a process spawned by the GitHub Actions Runner.Worker reading /proc/<pid>/maps or /proc/<pid>/mem to scrape CI/CD secrets, as seen in the simonecorsi/mawesome and tj-actions compromises.

detection:

source:linux.auditd @auditd.type:EXECVE @process.command_line:*/proc/* AND (@process.command_line:*maps* OR @process.command_line:*mem*)

| regex("/proc/[0-9a-z]+/(maps|mem)", field=CommandLine)

| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.parent_process_name="Runner.Worker" Processes.process="*/proc/*" by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | where match(process,"(?i)/proc/[0-9a-z]+/(maps|mem)") | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
First-seen external egress from GitHub Actions Runner.Worker child process AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts for CI/CD secret exfiltration: an interpreter or download tool spawned by Runner.Worker making an outbound connection to a public destination never seen from that runner population before. Targets the 'Credential Exfil' stage of the mawesome compromise. Rationale: Sysdig/Wiz note exfil variants that POST scraped secrets to gist.githubusercontent.com or attacker hosts; pivoting on a Runner.Worker child interpreter making a first-seen public connection isolates the exfil step. Sentinel/Datadog left blank because their available network tables in this tenant cannot attribute the connection back to the Runner.Worker parent process. Cross-checked against: • https://www.sysdig.com/blog/detecting-and-mitigating-the-tj-actions-changed-files-supply-chain-attack-cve-2025-30066 • https://www.wiz.io/blog/github-action-tj-actions-changed-files-supply-chain-attack-cve-2025-30066
ATT&CKT1567 T1041
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate workflow step that curls a public package registry or artifact host (pypi, npm, ghcr) for the first time
  • A build downloading a new dependency or container base image from an unseen CDN
  • Self-hosted runner first run after image rebuild hitting fresh update mirrors
  • Workflow posting results to a legitimate webhook (Slack/Datadog) not previously baselined
Suppression filter
| where not (RemoteUrl has_any ("pypi.org","files.pythonhosted.org","registry.npmjs.org","ghcr.io","objects.githubusercontent.com","github.com"))
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Inspect the destination (WHOIS/passive DNS) and the initiating command line — distinguish a known registry/CDN from an anonymous gist, paste, or raw IP. 2) CONTAIN: If the destination is attacker-controlled, isolate the runner, block the IP/domain at egress, and rotate every secret scoped to the job. 3) HUNT: Correlate the connection with a preceding Runner.Worker /proc memory-read event (UC2) and the known payload hash (UC1); review whether secrets were also echoed to the public job log.
let Baseline = DeviceNetworkEvents
    | where Timestamp between (ago(30d) .. ago(1d))
    | where InitiatingProcessParentFileName has "Runner.Worker"
    | summarize by RemoteUrl;
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessParentFileName has "Runner.Worker"
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("curl","wget","python3","python","node","sh","bash")
| join kind=leftanti Baseline on RemoteUrl
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, RemotePort

// Microsoft Sentinel — auto-derived from the Defender XDR hunt.

let Baseline = DeviceNetworkEvents
    | where TimeGenerated between (ago(30d) .. ago(1d))
    | where InitiatingProcessParentFileName has "Runner.Worker"
    | summarize by RemoteUrl;
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessParentFileName has "Runner.Worker"
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("curl","wget","python3","python","node","sh","bash")
| join kind=leftanti Baseline on RemoteUrl
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, RemotePort
| order by TimeGenerated desc
#event_simpleName=NetworkConnectIP4 RemotePort!=0
| NOT cidr("10.0.0.0/8", field=RemoteAddressIP4)

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("9f93d77d32833a515bc406c46da477142bb1ac2babeecb6aa42f98669a6db015", "5792aba0e2180b9b80b77644370a6889d5817456", "bcb6b1d409144318e8fad2171d6fe06d02299d1a") or SHA1 in~ ("9f93d77d32833a515bc406c46da477142bb1ac2babeecb6aa42f98669a6db015", "5792aba0e2180b9b80b77644370a6889d5817456", "bcb6b1d409144318e8fad2171d6fe06d02299d1a") or MD5 in~ ("9f93d77d32833a515bc406c46da477142bb1ac2babeecb6aa42f98669a6db015", "5792aba0e2180b9b80b77644370a6889d5817456", "bcb6b1d409144318e8fad2171d6fe06d02299d1a")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("9f93d77d32833a515bc406c46da477142bb1ac2babeecb6aa42f98669a6db015", "5792aba0e2180b9b80b77644370a6889d5817456", "bcb6b1d409144318e8fad2171d6fe06d02299d1a") or SHA1 in~ ("9f93d77d32833a515bc406c46da477142bb1ac2babeecb6aa42f98669a6db015", "5792aba0e2180b9b80b77644370a6889d5817456", "bcb6b1d409144318e8fad2171d6fe06d02299d1a") or MD5 in~ ("9f93d77d32833a515bc406c46da477142bb1ac2babeecb6aa42f98669a6db015", "5792aba0e2180b9b80b77644370a6889d5817456", "bcb6b1d409144318e8fad2171d6fe06d02299d1a")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["9f93d77d32833a515bc406c46da477142bb1ac2babeecb6aa42f98669a6db015", "5792aba0e2180b9b80b77644370a6889d5817456", "bcb6b1d409144318e8fad2171d6fe06d02299d1a"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

codfish/semantic-release-action GitHub Action has been compromised

StepSecurity
2026-07-01 10 use cases 3 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

On June 24, 2026, an attacker compromised the codfish/semantic-release-action GitHub repository. At 15:39:06 UTC they force-pushed a malicious commit and repointed several version tags to that commit. As a result, any workflow running against those tags after that time executed the attacker's code inside its GitHub Actions runner.

Malicious index.js dropped into codfish/semantic-release-action runner checkout AIDelivery Medium
Detects the compromised composite action being checked out onto a self-hosted GitHub Actions runner: the malicious commit ships a ~512KB index.js into the action's _actions checkout directory, whereas the legitimate action was Docker-based and only ever contained entrypoint.js + Dockerfile. Any index.js inside a codfish/semantic-release-action path (or matching the payload hash) indicates the hijacked tag was pulled. Rationale: Anchored on the article's exact facts: the action was converted Docker→composite and a 512KB index.js was added under the action path (_actions/codfish/semantic-release-action). Legit versions never contained index.js, making path+filename and the payload SHA256 (9f93d77d...) high-fidelity. Corroborated by Aikido's independent write-up. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/supply-chain-compromise-codfish-semantic-release-action • https://www.aikido.dev/blog/compromised-github-action-codfish-steals-secrets • https://github.com/codfish/semantic-release-action/activity
ATT&CKT1195.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A downstream fork that legitimately re-bundles the action as a Node/Bun composite with its own index.js
  • Security researchers replaying the malicious commit in a sandbox runner for analysis
  • Internal mirror/cache of GitHub Actions that retains the old malicious artifact after remediation
  • An unrelated action in a different org that happens to share the 'semantic-release-action' substring in its name
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("defender", "mssense.exe") and FolderPath !has "\\analysis-sandbox\\"
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Confirm the FolderPath resolves to a GitHub Actions _actions checkout and the file SHA256 = 9f93d77d...; identify which workflow/repo on this runner referenced codfish/semantic-release-action and which tag (v1.6.1–v2.2.1) it pinned. 2) CONTAIN: Take the self-hosted runner offline, rotate every secret that workflow could touch (GITHUB_TOKEN is auto-expired but rotate any NPM_TOKEN/PAT/cloud OIDC trust), and revoke OIDC sessions. 3) HUNT: Pin the action to the clean v5 SHA across the org, search other runners for the same file/hash, and look for the Bun execution and dead-drop C2 (UCs below) on the same host.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| where (FolderPath has "semantic-release-action" and FileName =~ "index.js")
   or SHA256 =~ "9f93d77d32833a515bc406c46da477142bb1ac2babeecb6aa42f98669a6db015"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FolderPath, FileName, SHA256, FileSize, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventType == "FileCreated"
| where (TargetFilePath has "semantic-release-action" and TargetFileName =~ "index.js")
   or TargetFileSHA256 =~ "9f93d77d32833a515bc406c46da477142bb1ac2babeecb6aa42f98669a6db015"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, TargetFileSHA256, ActingProcessName, ActorUsername
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Bun runtime executing payload index.js from semantic-release-action path AIInstallation High
Detects the malicious composite action's injected step running the payload via `bun run <action_path>/index.js`. The attacker deliberately chose Bun over Node to evade Node's --require security hooks. A Bun process whose command line references both the codfish/semantic-release-action path and index.js is the execution stage of the compromise. Rationale: Uses the article's exact execution string `bun run ${{ github.action_path }}/index.js` — the path token 'semantic-release-action' + 'index.js' + the Bun binary is unique to this compromise (legit action ran node /action/entrypoint.js in Docker). The Bun choice for --require evasion is called out explicitly in the article. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/supply-chain-compromise-codfish-semantic-release-action • https://www.aikido.dev/blog/compromised-github-action-codfish-steals-secrets

  • A CI smoke-test that intentionally executes the action's index.js for regression testing
  • Security tooling detonating the sample in a controlled runner

1) TRIAGE: Confirm the Bun command line points at a github.com _actions/codfish/semantic-release-action checkout and capture the parent (Runner.Worker/bash) and the host. 2) CONTAIN: Isolate the runner, kill the Bun process, and immediately rotate all CI/CD secrets reachable by that job (GITHUB_TOKEN, NPM_TOKEN, cloud OIDC role trust) — Aikido reports the payload reads Runner.Worker memory to steal secrets in flight. 3) HUNT: On the same host pivot to the dead-drop C2 UC (GitHub commit-search) and to any git pushes/commits the stolen token made to other repos (worm self-propagation).

| order by Timestamp desc

GitHub dead-drop C2 — commit-search for RevokeAndItGoesKaboom / TheBeautifulSandsOfTime AICommand & Control Medium
Detects the payload's dead-drop C2: it queries the GitHub commit-search API for messages tagged RevokeAndItGoesKaboom (encrypted operator PAT) and TheBeautifulSandsOfTime (RSA-signed eval command). On a TLS-inspecting proxy these unique markers appear verbatim in the request URL; on raw EDR, surface the Bun process resolving/connecting to api.github.com for the same purpose. Rationale: Uses the article's verbatim dead-drop identifiers (RevokeAndItGoesKaboom, TheBeautifulSandsOfTime) and the exact search endpoint /search/commits?q=RevokeAndItGoesKaboom — proxy-visible markers are near-zero FP. The Defender/Falcon variants degrade gracefully to 'Bun reaching api.github.com' since HTTPS hides the query string. Datadog/Sigma omitted: no native GitHub/proxy source maps cleanly to the URL-marker logic and it is multi-shape across telemetry. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/supply-chain-compromise-codfish-semantic-release-action • https://www.aikido.dev/blog/compromised-github-action-codfish-steals-secrets
ATT&CKT1102.001 T1528
Data sourcesWeb.Web Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate Bun-based tooling that calls the GitHub API during a release (Defender/Falcon variant only)
  • A developer manually searching GitHub commits containing the string 'RevokeAndItGoesKaboom' while researching this incident
  • Threat-intel platforms or scanners crawling GitHub commit search
  • Proxy logging a researcher's reproduction traffic in a sandbox
Suppression filter
| where SrcHostname !has "sandbox" and UserAgent !has "ThreatIntel"
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: For proxy hits, confirm the URL contains the literal dead-drop marker and the source is a CI runner/Bun host — that is a confirmed C2 callback. For EDR-only hits, verify the Bun process correlates with the index.js execution UC on the same host/time. 2) CONTAIN: Isolate the runner, block egress, and revoke/rotate every token the runner held; assume the operator already pulled a stolen PAT via the dead drop. 3) HUNT: Search org-wide GitHub audit logs for commits/pushes made by stolen tokens, new commits matching RevokeAndItGoesKaboom: or TheBeautifulSandsOfTime: in your repos, and the same campaign fingerprint in @antv/graphlib, echarts-for-react, and tanstack-react-router dependencies.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "bun"
| where RemoteUrl has "github.com" or RemoteUrl has "githubusercontent.com"
| summarize ConnCount=count(), FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), Urls=make_set(RemoteUrl,20) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP
| order by FirstSeen desc
// HTTPS hides the ?q=RevokeAndItGoesKaboom query string at the network layer; this surfaces Bun talking to GitHub for triage. Use ImWebSession/proxy for the verbatim marker.
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Url has_any ("RevokeAndItGoesKaboom","TheBeautifulSandsOfTime","search/commits?q=RevokeAndItGoesKaboom")
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname, SrcUsername, Url, UserAgent=HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent, DstIpAddr, DstHostname
| order by TimeGenerated desc
#event_simpleName=DnsRequest
| DomainName=/(^|\.)github\.com$/i
| ContextImageFileName=/bun/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, DomainName], function=count())
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Web.Web where (Web.url="*RevokeAndItGoesKaboom*" OR Web.url="*TheBeautifulSandsOfTime*" OR Web.url="*search/commits?q=RevokeAndItGoesKaboom*") by Web.src Web.user Web.dest Web.url Web.http_user_agent | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Web.Web where (Web.url="*RevokeAndItGoesKaboom*" OR Web.url="*TheBeautifulSandsOfTime*" OR Web.url="*search/commits?q=RevokeAndItGoesKaboom*") by Web.src Web.user Web.dest Web.url Web.http_user_agent | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
